column4: فَاسْعَوْا commands people to hasten toward Friday remembrance and leave trade; the same sa'y word now gathers them toward one shared direction.
After prayer, people are told to disperse through the land and seek God's bounty; this reverses the gathering of 62:9 and closely recalls people leaving one watering place for separate aims.

Righteousness is not merely turning faces east or west; the verse defines it through belief, giving wealth, keeping promises, and patience. It links the section's qibla/direction gloss to its moral course of giving.
The question about the changed qibla and the statement that God guides whom He wills to a straight way connect physical orientation with the section's hidaya-as-direction gloss.
The verse says the former qibla was a test of who follows the Messenger; it makes turning toward a direction a choice that reveals one's course.
The command to face the Sacred Mosque wherever one is supplies the physical qibla orientation named alongside direction in the section's hidaya dictionary note.
The choice “whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve” is followed by the fire prepared for wrongdoers, explicitly dividing human courses and outcomes.
The Hour is coming so that every soul may be repaid for what it strives for; this directly joins the section's striving to its final reckoning.
The question introduces the greatest losers in deeds; 18:104 identifies their lost effort and mistaken confidence.
سَعْيُهُمْ فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا names efforts lost in worldly life even while their agents think they act well, a direct contrary path to the section's fruitful striving.
The next verse says those losers denied their Lord's signs and meeting Him, explaining the wasted deeds announced in 18:104.
God begins creation and repeats it, with all returning to Him; this gives a creation-to-return arc beside the section's first and last and its race endpoint.
The verse tells the Messenger that he cannot guide whom he loves, while God guides whom He wills; it specifies divine responsibility in the guidance claim.
Believers are told to fear God, seek a means to Him, and strive in His way; the verse brings taqwa, directed effort, and a path into one command.
Satan says he will sit on God's straight path to obstruct it, making opposition to the guided course explicit.
Satan's approach from before, behind, right, and left recalls the section's dictionary list of direction, front, and back; it shows temptation coming from every side of the path.
God opens one person's chest to Islam but makes another's constricted as though climbing heaven; this gives an inward experience of ease and difficulty alongside the section's route metaphor.
The verse says disbelievers' wealth and children will not avail them against God and names the Fire; this directly echoes the section's question about wealth when a person falls.
The same wealth-and-children formula is applied to disbelievers and followed by the Fire, restating the section's limit on wealth at the end of a course.
Wealth and children will not avail people against God, and they are assigned to the Fire; this is another direct formulation of the failure of wealth in the section's reckoning.
Those who hoard gold and silver without spending in God's way are warned of painful punishment, a direct opposite to the section's giver and a concrete form of miserliness.
The next verse says the hoarded metal will be heated and used to brand its owners, then calls it what they hoarded; it makes the miser's wealth itself part of the outcome.
After receiving God's bounty, these people became miserly and turned away; it joins the section's bukhul and tawalla in one account.
The verse condemns those who withhold God's bounty and calls their assumed good evil; it directly develops the miser's path and its reversal.
It names the stingy, those who urge others to stinginess, and those who conceal God's bounty; this adds concealment and social influence to the section's miserly course.
This verse describes the stingy and those who urge stinginess, then says God is self-sufficient; it exposes the false human self-sufficiency paired with withholding in the section.
Spend from what God provided and whoever is protected from the greed of his own soul succeeds; this directly reverses the section's miserly path.
The verse says people would still withhold even if they owned the treasuries of their Lord's mercy; it gives a concrete form to the section's self-sufficient miser.
The warning not to let wealth and children distract from God's remembrance fits the section's self-sufficient person whose wealth cannot save him.
People are urged to spend from what God provided before death comes, a precise link to the section's giver and its warning about the moment a person falls.
The next verse says no soul's appointed time is delayed and God knows what people do, completing the urgency of spending before death in 63:10.
Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminders or injury receive reward from their Lord; this directly explains the section's giver who has no favor to be repaid.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, specifying the contrast between sincere giving and a gift used to claim a favor.
Those who spend seeking God's approval and to strengthen themselves are compared to a garden on high ground; the motive directly parallels the section's gift for the Lord's face.
Men and women who give charity are promised multiplied reward, a direct giving-to-recompense parallel to the section's course.
Neither wealth nor children bring people near to God; belief and righteous action do, with multiplied reward. This directly distinguishes the section's wealth from the effort that reaches its end.
Those who spend in ease and hardship are described as God-fearing, joining the section's generosity with its two conditions and its taqwa.
The God-fearing are said to reserve a right in their wealth for the asker and deprived, specifying the generosity of the pious course.
